readings.c1s1: certain. Various explanations have been offered: (1) < ME. ''bagge'', a bag (because beggars carry bags: see first quotation under ''beggar'', ''n.''); but this is certainly wrong. It would imply the forms *''beggen'', *''begge'', as variants of ''baggen'', ''bagge'', but no such variants are found or are probable, and no such sense as ‘put into a bag,’ or ‘carry a bag,’ which might connect the notion of ‘bag’ with that of ‘beg,’ belongs to the ME. verb ''baggen'', which is found only in the sense of ‘swell out like a bag’; the sense of ‘put into a bag’ is modern, and that of ‘carry a bag’ does not exist; ''bagger'', moreover, the supposed antecedent of ''beggar'', is only modern. (2) < AS. ''bedecian'', beg (connected with Goth. ''bidagwa'', a beggar, appar. < ''bidjan'' = AS. ''biddan'', E. ''bid'', ask; cf. D. ''bedelen'' = OHG. ''betalōn'', MHG. ''betelen'', G. ''betteln'', beg, freq. of D. ''bidden'' = G. ''bitten'' = AS. ''biddan'', E. ''bid'', ask); but the AS. ''bedecian'' occurs but once, in the 9th century, and there are no intermediate forms to connect it with ME. ''beggen''. (3) < OFlem. *''beggen'', beg; but there is no such word. (4) < OF. ''beg-'', the common radical of ''begard'', ''begart'', ''beguard'', ''begar'' (ML. ''begardus'', ''beggardus'', ''beghardus'', etc.), and ''beguin'' (ML. ''beginus'', ''begginus'', ''beghinus'', ''beguinus'', etc.), names given to the members of a mendicant lay brotherhood (see ''Beghard'' and ''Beguin''); also applied to any begging friar or other

'''beggar-weed''' (beg′ä̤r-wēd), ''n.'' [Cf. ''beggary''<sup>2</sup>, 2.] A name sometimes given in England to the common door-weed, ''Polygonum aviculare'', to ''Cuscuta Trifolii'', and to some other plants.

'''beggary'''<sup>1</sup> (beg′ä̤r-i), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''beggery'', < ME. ''beggerie'', < ''beggere'', beggar.] '''1.''' The state of a beggar; a condition of extreme indigence.
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis the narrowness of human nature,
Our poverty and ''beggary'' of spirit,
To take exception at these things.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', The New Inn, iv. 3.}}
His vessel with an inestimable cargo has just gone down, and he is reduced in a moment from opulence to ''beggary''. {{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}}
'''2†.''' The act or practice of begging; the occupation of a beggar; begging.
{{smaller block|We must be careful that our charity do not minister to idleness and the love of ''beggary''.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Great Exemplar.}}}}
'''3.''' Beggars collectively; beggardom; beggarhood.
{{smaller block|The Piazza is invaded by the legions of ''beggary'', and held in overpowering numbers against all comers.
{{right|''Howells'', Venetian Life, xviii.}}}}
'''4.''' A state of bareness or deficiency.
{{smaller block|The freedom and the ''beggary'' of the old studio.
{{right|''Thackeray''.}}}}

'''beggary'''<sup>2</sup> (beg′ä̤r-i), ''a.'' [< ''beggar'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Beggarly; poor; mean. [Rare.]—'''2.''' Full of weeds. [Local, Eng.]

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|beg|506|beggary}}</noinclude>certain. Various explanations have been offered: (1) < ME. ''bagge'', a bag (because beggars carry bags: see first quotation under ''beggar'', ''n.''); but this is certainly wrong. It would imply the forms *''beggen'', *''begge'', as variants of ''baggen'', ''bagge'', but no such variants are found or are probable, and no such sense as ‘put into a bag,’ or ‘carry a bag,’ which might connect the notion of ‘bag’ with that of ‘beg,’ belongs to the ME. verb ''baggen'', which is found only in the sense of ‘swell out like a bag’; the sense of ‘put into a bag’ is modern, and that of ‘carry a bag’ does not exist; ''bagger'', moreover, the supposed antecedent of ''beggar'', is only modern. (2) < AS. ''bedecian'', beg (connected with Goth. ''bidagwa'', a beggar, appar. < ''bidjan'' = AS. ''biddan'', E. ''bid'', ask; cf. D. ''bedelen'' = OHG. ''betalōn'', MHG. ''betelen'', G. ''betteln'', beg, freq. of D. ''bidden'' = G. ''bitten'' = AS. ''biddan'', E. ''bid'', ask); but the AS. ''bedecian'' occurs but once, in the 9th century, and there are no intermediate forms to connect it with ME. ''beggen''. (3) < OFlem. *''beggen'', beg; but there is no such word. (4) < OF. ''beg-'', the common radical of ''begard'', ''begart'', ''beguard'', ''begar'' (ML. ''begardus'', ''beggardus'', ''beghardus'', etc.), and ''beguin'' (ML. ''beginus'', ''begginus'', ''beghinus'', ''beguinus'', etc.), names given to the members of a mendicant lay brotherhood (see ''Beghard'' and ''Beguin''); also applied to any begging friar or other beggar. Such mendicants were very numerous at the time of the first appearance of the E. verb, and the derived OF. verb ''beguiner'', ''beguigner'' (< ''beguin''), with AF. ''begger'', is actually found in the sense of ‘beg.’ The E. verb may be a back formation from the noun ''beggar'' (ME. ''begger'', ''beggere'', ''beggar'', ''beggare''), which is, in this view, an adapted form (as if a noun of agent in ''-ar''<sup>1</sup>, ''-er''<sup>1</sup>) of the OF. ''begar'', ''begard'', etc., a Beghard. ''Beghard'' is otherwise not found in ME., though the precise form ''begger'' is found in Wyclif and later as a designation of the mendicant friars (Beghards), appar. without direct reference to their begging.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To ask for or supplicate in charity; ask as alms.
{{smaller block|Yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed ''begging'' bread.
{{right|Ps. xxxvii. 25.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For all thy blessed youth
Becomes as aged, and doth ''beg'' the alms
Of palsied eld.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To ask for earnestly; crave.
{{smaller block|He [Joseph] . . . ''begged'' the body of Jesus.
{{right|Mat. xxvii. 58.}}}}
'''3.''' To ask as a favor; hence, to beseech; entreat or supplicate with humility or earnestness: as, I ''begged'' him to use his influence in favor of my friend.
{{smaller block|<poem>And on our knees we ''beg''
(As recompense of our dear services,
Past and to come) that you do change this purpose.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 3.}}}}
'''To beg a person for a fool†''', {{smaller|to take him for, or regard him as, a fool.}}
{{smaller block|In the old common law was a writ . . . under which if a man was legally proved an idiot, the profit of his lands . . . might be granted by the king to any subject. . . . Such a person, when this grant was asked, was said ''to be begged for a fool.''
{{right|''Nares.''}}}}

{{smaller|'''To beg the question''', in ''logic'', to assume or take as granted that which is not more certain than the proposition to be proved, or which obviously involves the point in question; assume as a premise what no one who takes the opposite view of the question will admit.}}

{{smaller block|The sophism of ''begging the question'' is, then, when any thing is proved either by itself or something that is equally unknown with itself.
{{right|''Burgersdicius'', tr. by a Gentleman (1697).}}}}
{{smaller block|The attempt to infer his [Shakspere’s] classical education from the internal evidence of his works is simply a ''begging of the question.''
{{right|''G. P. Marsh'', Lects. on Eng. Lang., p. 82.}}}}
{{smaller block|To maintain, as Sir Wyville Thomson does, that 32° is the temperature of the floor on which the Antarctic ice-sheet rests, is virtually ''to beg the question.''
{{right|''J. Croll'', Climate and Cosmology, p. 226.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Ask, Request, Beg'', etc. (see ''ask''<sup>1</sup>); to pray (for), conjure, petition (for).}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To ask alms or charity; practise begging; live by asking alms.

{{smaller block|I cannot dig; to ''beg'' I am ashamed.
{{right|Luke xvi. 3.}}}}

'''2.''' In the game of all-fours, to ask of the dealer a concession of one point to be added to one’s count. {{smaller|The dealer must either concede the point or deal out three additional cards to each player. Should the suit originally turned as trump appear after this new deal, three, or fewer if so agreed, must be dealt to each until a different trump appears.—'''To beg off''', to obtain release from a penalty, obligation, etc., by entreaty or excuses.}}

'''beg<sup>2</sup>''' (beg), ''n.'' Same as ''bey''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bega, biggah''' (bē′gä, big′ä), ''n.''   [Also written ''beega, beegah, beegha'', etc., repr. Hind. ''bighā'', Marathi ''bigha''.]   A Hindu land-measure, locally varying in extent, but usually regarded as equal to from one third to two thirds of an English acre. The bega of Calcutta is 1,600 square yards, or about a third of an acre.

'''begad''' (bē-gad′), ''interj.''   [A minced oath, a corruption of ''by God!'' Cf. ''egad, bedad.'']   A sort of exclamatory oath, employed to give weight to a statement.
{{smaller block|''Begad'', madam, . . . ’tis the very same I met.
{{right|''Fielding'', Joseph Andrews.}}}}

'''begall''' (bē-gâl′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gall''<sup>2</sup>.]   To gall; fret; chafe; rub sore.   ''Bp. Hall.''

'''began''' (bē-gan′). Preterit of ''begin.''

'''begat''' (bē-gat′). Old preterit of ''beget'', still sometimes used poetically.

'''begaud†''' (bē-gâd′), ''v. t.''   [Also written ''begawd''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gaud'': see ''gaud''<sup>1</sup>.]   To bedeck with gaudy things.   ''North.''

'''begaum''', ''n.'' See ''begum''<sup>2</sup>.

'''begeck†''' (bē-gek′), ''v. t.''   [Sc., also ''begeek'' (= D. ''begekken''); < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''geck.'' Cf. ''begunk.'']   To befool; gull; jilt.   ''N. E. D.''

'''begem''' (bē-jem′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''begemmed'', ppr. ''begemming.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gem.'']   To adorn with gems, or as with gems; stud with gems, or anything suggesting them.
{{smaller block|<poem>The lawn
''Begemmed'' with dew-drops.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., iii. 2.}}}}

'''beget''' (bē-get′), ''v. t.''; pret. ''begot'', formerly ''begat'', pp. ''begotten'', ''begot'', ppr. ''begetting''. [< ME. ''begeten'', ''begiten'', ''bigiten'', etc., < AS. ''begitan'', ''bigitan'' (= OS. ''bigitan'' = OHG. ''bigezan''), get, acquire, < ''be-'' + ''gitan'', ''getan'', get: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''get''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To procreate; generate: chiefly used of the father alone, but sometimes of both parents.
{{smaller block|Abraham ''begat'' Isaac; and Isaac ''begat'' Jacob; and Jacob ''begat'' Judas and his brethren.
{{right|Mat. i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Yet they a beauteous offspring shall ''beget''.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 613.}}}}
{{smaller block|Become stout Marses, and ''beget'' young Cupids.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, ii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To produce as an effect; cause to exist; generate; occasion: as, luxury ''begets'' vice; “love is ''begot'' by fancy,” ''Glanville''.
{{smaller block|Intellectual science has been observed to ''beget'' invariably a doubt of the existence of matter.
{{right|''Emerson'', Nature.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thought is essentially independent of language, and speech could never have ''begotten'' reason.
{{right|''Mivart'', Nature and Thought, p. 167.}}}}
='''Syn.''' To breed, engender.

'''begetter''' (bē-get′ėr), ''n.'' One who begets or procreates; a father.

'''begetting''' (bē-get′ing), ''n.'' '''1.''' The act of procreating or producing.—'''2.''' That which is begotten; progeny.

'''beggable''' (beg′a̤-bl), ''a.''   [< ''beg''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able''.]   Capable of being begged.
{{smaller block|Things disposed of or not ''beggable''.
{{right|''Butler'', Characters.}}}}

'''beggar''' (beg′ä̤r), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. more commonly ''begger'', < ME. ''begger'', ''beggere'', also ''beggar'', ''beggare'', a beggar: for the etym., see ''beg''<sup>1</sup>. The reg. mod. spelling is ''begger''; the ME. variant spelling ''beggar'', ''beggare'', has not necessarily a bearing upon the conjectured derivation from OF. ''begard'', the suffix ''-er'' being in ME. often variable to ''-ar''; cf. mod. E. ''liar''.]   '''1.''' One who begs or asks alms; especially, one who lives by asking alms or makes it his business to beg.
{{smaller block|<poem>Bidderes and ''beggeres'' fast about yede,
With hire belies and here bagges of brede full ycrammed.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman.''}}}}
'''2.''' One who is in indigent circumstances; one who has been beggared.—'''3†.''' One who asks a favor; one who entreats; a petitioner.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Count.'' Wilt thou needs be a ''beggar''?
''Clo.'' I do beg your good-will in this case.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>What subjects will precarious kings regard?
A ''beggar'' speaks too softly to be heard. ''Dryden.''</poem>}}
'''4.''' One who assumes in argument what he does not prove.
{{smaller block|These shameful ''beggars'' of principles.
{{right|''Tillotson.''}}}}
'''5.''' A fellow; a rogue: used (''a'') in contempt for a low fellow; (''b'') as a term of playful familiarity: as, he is a good-hearted little ''beggar''.—'''Masterful beggar.''' {{smaller|See ''masterful''.}}—'''To go''' {{smaller|or}} '''go home by beggar’s bush''', {{smaller|to go to ruin.   ''Brewer.''}}

'''beggar''' (beg′ä̤r), ''v. t.''   [Early mod. E. also ''begger''; < ''beggar'', ''n.'']   '''1.''' To make a beggar of; reduce to beggary; impoverish.
<poem>Whose heavy hand hath bow’d you to the grave,
And ''beggar’d'' yours for ever.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 1.}}}}
<poem>''Beggar’d'' by fools, whom still he found too late;
He had his jest, and they had his estate.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dryden'', Abs. and Achit., i. 561.}}}}

{{smaller block|A rapacious government, and a ''beggared'' exchequer.
{{right|''Buckle'', Civilization, I. 653.}}}}
'''2.''' To exhaust the resources of; exceed the means or capacity of; outdo.

{{smaller block|When the two heroes met, then began a scene of warlike parade that ''beggars'' all description.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 328.}}}}

{{smaller block|Shakespeare carries us to such a lofty strain of intelligent activity as to suggest a wealth which ''beggars'' his own.
{{right|''Emerson'', Essays, 1st ser., p. 262.}}}}

'''beggardom''' (beg′ä̤r-dum), ''n.'' The state of beggary; the body or fraternity of beggars.

'''beggarhood''' (beg′ä̤r-hu̇d), ''n.''   [< ''beggar'' + ''-hood.'']   The character or state of being a beggar; beggars collectively.

'''beggarism''' (beg′ä̤r-izm), ''n.''   [< ''beggar'' + ''-ism.'']   The state or condition of beggary.

'''beggarliness''' (beg′ä̤r-li-nes), ''n.''   [< ''beggarly'' + ''-ness.'']   The state of being beggarly; extreme poverty; meanness.

'''beggarly''' (beg′ä̤r-li), ''a.''   [Early mod. E. also ''beggerly''; < ''beggar'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' In the condition of or becoming a beggar; extremely indigent; poor; mean; contemptible: used of persons and things.

{{smaller block|A ''beggarly'' account of empty boxes.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., v. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Beggarly'' sins, that is, those sins which idleness and beggary usually betray men to, such as lying, flattery, stealing, and dissimulation.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor.''}}}}

{{smaller block|He was an idle, ''beggarly'' fellow, and of no use to the public.
{{right|''Addison'', Trial of Punctilios.}}}} '''2.''' Of or for beggars. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|But moralists, sociologists, political economists, and taxes have slowly convinced me that my ''beggarly'' sympathies were a sin against society.
{{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 59.}}}}

'''beggarly†''' (beg′ä̤r-li), ''adv.'' Meanly; indigently; despicably.

{{smaller block|It is his delight to dwell ''beggarly.''
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Pol., v. § 15.}}}}

'''beggar-my-neighbor''' (beg′ä̤r-mī-nā′bo̤r), ''n.''   [In allusion to the continued loss of cards.]   A children’s game at cards. {{smaller|In one variety of it the players hold the cards with the backs upward, and alternately lay one down till an honor is turned up, which has to be paid for at the rate of four cards for an ace, three for a king, etc.; and the game goes on thus till one has gained all the other’s cards.}}

'''beggar’s-basket''' (beg′ä̤rz-bȧs″ket), ''n.'' The European lungwort, ''Pulmonaria officinalis.''

'''beggar’s-lice''' (beg′ä̤rz-līs), ''n.'' '''1.''' An English name of ''Galium Aparine'', or goose-grass, given to it because its burs stick to the clothes, and somewhat resemble lice.—'''2.''' The name given in the United States to species of ''Bidens'' and to ''Echinospermum Virginicum'', the seeds of which have barbed awns which cling persistently to clothing. Also called ''beggar’s-ticks.''

'''beggar’s-needle''' (beg′ä̤rz-nē″dl), ''n.'' An English popular name for the ''Scandix Pecten'', from its long-beaked fronds.

'''beggar’s-ticks''' (beg′ä̤rz-tiks), ''n.'' Same as ''beggar’s-lice'', 2. Also written ''beggarticks.''

{{smaller block|It [the garden] was over-run with Roman wormwood and ''beggarticks'', which last stuck to my clothes.
{{right|''Thoreau'', Walden, p. 282.}}}}

'''beggar-weed''' (beg′ä̤r-wēd), ''n.''   [Cf. ''beggary''<sup>2</sup>, 2.]   A name sometimes given in England to the common door-weed, ''Polygonum aviculare'', to ''Cuscuta Trifolii'', and to some other plants.

'''beggary'''<sup>1</sup> (beg′ä̤r-i), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''beggery'', < ME. ''beggerie'', < ''beggere'', beggar.]   '''1.''' The state of a beggar; a condition of extreme indigence.
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis the narrowness of human nature,
Our poverty and ''beggary'' of spirit,
To take exception at these things.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', The New Inn, iv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|His vessel with an inestimable cargo has just gone down, and he is reduced in a moment from opulence to ''beggary''. {{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}}
'''2†.''' The act or practice of begging; the occupation of a beggar; begging.
{{smaller block|We must be careful that our charity do not minister to idleness and the love of ''beggary''.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Great Exemplar.}}}}
'''3.''' Beggars collectively; beggardom; beggarhood.
{{smaller block|The Piazza is invaded by the legions of ''beggary'', and held in overpowering numbers against all comers.
{{right|''Howells'', Venetian Life, xviii.}}}}
'''4.''' A state of bareness or deficiency.
{{smaller block|The freedom and the ''beggary'' of the old studio.
{{right|''Thackeray''.}}}}

'''beggary'''<sup>2</sup> (beg′ä̤r-i), ''a.''   [< ''beggar'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Beggarly; poor; mean. [Rare.]—'''2.''' Full of weeds. [Local, Eng.]<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
